strengths: Introduces a new resource, SciEvents, targeting a genuinely underexplored domain (scientific abstracts) for document-level, multi-event extraction with hierarchical (sub-event) structure and non-flat (overlapping/inconsecutive/reverse-ordered) arguments, addressing a real gap in EE datasets.

The annotation process is reasonably rigorous and documented: multi-round schema design with domain experts, staged annotator training/screening, quality inspection with conflict-based revision loops, and reported cost/time statistics, which supports reproducibility of the dataset construction.

The dataset statistics (nugget density, argument length, proportion of complex nugget forms, sub-event proportion) are compared against several existing benchmarks (ACE2005, RAMS, WIKIEVENTS, DICE), providing quantitative evidence that SciEvents differs meaningfully from prior EE datasets in the dimensions the paper claims to target.

The proposed EXCEEDS architecture is a coherent technical contribution that unifies event detection, argument extraction, and event correlation (hierarchy) prediction within a single word-word grid formulation, extending prior word-word relation classification work to handle global-range HTL (reverse-ordered nuggets) and event-argument/event-event links.

Empirical results show consistent improvements over multiple representative baselines (OneIE, BartGen, UIE, PAIE) across all reported metrics, including the newly proposed event correlation (EC) metric for hierarchical events, and an ablation study isolates the contribution of the Biaffine and BiAttention modules.

The new EC metric is a useful, well-motivated complement to standard trigger/argument metrics for evaluating hierarchical/nested event extraction, and the paper provides a clear worked example clarifying metric computation.
weaknesses: The dataset is derived exclusively from ACL main conference paper abstracts (2019-2022), which is a narrow slice of 'scientific domain' (essentially NLP/CL papers only); claims of being a general 'scientific domain' dataset are overstated given this single-subfield, single-venue sourcing, and generalization to other scientific disciplines (biology, physics, chemistry, etc.) is untested.

No inter-annotator agreement (IAA) statistics are reported despite an elaborate annotation pipeline; without IAA (e.g., Cohen's kappa, F1 agreement between annotators) it is hard to assess the reliability/consistency of the complex, schema-heavy annotations, which is a significant reproducibility and soundness gap for a paper whose main claimed contribution is a benchmark dataset.

The overall absolute performance of EXCEEDS remains low (e.g., AC F1 ~41.85%, EC F1 ~47.60%), and the paper does not sufficiently discuss error analysis or qualitative failure cases beyond aggregate numbers, limiting insight into whether the proposed grid-based method genuinely resolves the density/complexity challenges or merely improves marginally over baselines while still performing poorly in absolute terms.

Baseline comparisons may be somewhat unfair or incompletely described: BartGen and PAIE rely on an externally trained ED module (the cited word-word relation classifier) for inference, which conflates method contributions, and OneIE reportedly uses additional entity annotations during training that other models (including EXCEEDS presumably) do not use, complicating fair comparison; no LLM-based baselines (e.g., GPT-4, zero/few-shot LLMs) are included despite these being highlighted as the state of the art in the related work discussion.

The complex-nuggets/events scenario analysis (Table 4) contains apparent inconsistencies (e.g., text claims an EC F1 of 15.79 for Inconsecutive Nugget that does not appear in Table 4, which only reports EC for Sub-event), suggesting errors or omissions in reporting that undermine confidence in the presented results.

The paper lacks statistical significance testing or variance/standard deviation reporting despite stating results are averaged over at least three runs, making it hard to judge whether the reported improvements over baselines are robust rather than due to run-to-run variance.

Method novelty is somewhat incremental: the core word-word grid formulation is adapted from prior NER-as-word-word-relation-classification work (Li et al. 2022) and CLN from Liu et al. 2021, with the main technical additions being extension to global HTL range and added BiAttention/EAL relations; the individual architectural contributions (Biaffine, BiAttention) yield only modest ablation gains (e.g., 0.34 F1 drop for BiAttention removal on AC), raising questions about how much each component matters versus simply having a unified grid.

There is no human evaluation, external validity check, or comparison of the schema's coverage/soundness against alternative existing IE schemas for scientific text (e.g., SciERC, similar scientific NLP resources), leaving unclear how well-justified or comprehensive the specific event/argument taxonomy is relative to alternatives.

Reproducibility for the method is only partially supported in the main text (some hyperparameters and architecture details are given, but full training configuration, code availability confirmation within the review copy, and computational cost are not thoroughly detailed within the visible manuscript).

strengths: Addresses a genuine gap: no prior document-level, multi-event extraction dataset exists for the scientific literature domain, and the paper backs up the claimed 'denser and more complex' characteristics with clear comparative statistics (NugProp, ArgToken, Tokens/Events) against ACE2005, RAMS, WIKIEVENTS, and DICE.

The annotation pipeline is described with unusual rigor for a resource paper (director training, staged annotator screening, weekly quality review, conflict-triggered re-annotation), which supports reproducibility of the process even if agreement statistics are missing.

The proposed schema explicitly models phenomena that are typically ignored in standard IE schemas (non-flat/overlapping/reverse-ordered nuggets, hierarchical sub-events), and the paper quantifies the prevalence of each phenomenon (Table 2), motivating the method design.

EXCEEDS is a reasonably well-motivated unification of word-word grid tagging (NER-as-relation) with biaffine and bi-attention modules to jointly handle nugget extraction, argument linking, and event hierarchy in one grid, avoiding pipeline error propagation.

Empirical results are consistent across the main table, the complex-scenario breakdown (Table 4), and the ablation (Table 5), and EXCEEDS outperforms all baselines on nearly every metric, with a particularly large margin on hierarchical event correlation (EC), which is the paper's distinguishing contribution.
Introduction of the EC metric to specifically evaluate hierarchical/sub-event extraction is a useful methodological addition that other document-level EE work has generally lacked.
weaknesses: No inter-annotator agreement (IAA) statistics are reported anywhere in the paper despite the elaborate annotation pipeline; for a dataset-contribution paper this is a significant omission that leaves annotation quality/schema reliability unverified.

The dataset is built exclusively from ACL conference paper abstracts (NLP subfield only), yet the paper repeatedly frames the contribution as covering the 'scientific domain' broadly; this is an overclaim, and it is unclear whether the schema, templates, or empirical findings generalize to other sciences (biology, physics, chemistry) with different abstract conventions.

Absolute performance is quite low across all metrics (best AC F1 ≈ 42%, best inconsecutive/reverse-ordered nugget F1 in the teens), and the paper does not provide qualitative error analysis or discussion of whether this reflects genuine task difficulty, schema/annotation noise, or model limitations — this matters for judging whether the dataset is well-posed.

No LLM-based baselines (GPT-4/instruction-tuned IE models) are included despite the related-work section extensively discussing LLM-based EE approaches; given how central LLMs are to current IE research, their absence weakens the completeness of the comparison.

The event/argument schema is built around fixed natural-language templates per event type (Appendix A), which risks being a rigid, somewhat ad hoc design tied closely to the specific abstract-writing conventions observed by the annotators; robustness/generality of this schema to abstracts with different rhetorical structures is untested.

Results are reported as averages over 'at least three experiments' with no variance/standard deviation or significance testing, making it hard to assess how robust the reported state-of-the-art margins are, especially given some are small (e.g., TC F1 63.11 vs 59.88 for OneIE, AC 41.85 vs 39.83 for PAIE).

Reproducibility details for dataset licensing/release and precise data splits/preprocessing (e.g., how sub-events are represented in released format) are thin; while code/data are claimed to be released on GitHub, the paper itself does not describe format specifics beyond Appendix B.

Writing has several typos and rough phrasing (e.g., 'Statisics', 'threes kinds') and repeated over-interpretation of routine statistics (e.g., long qualitative narrative about argument-type distributions) that could be tightened.

strengths: Introduces SciEvents, a large-scale, richly annotated document-level event extraction dataset (2,508 docs, 24,381 events, 56,411 arguments) with a carefully engineered schema tailored to capture hierarchical relations, discontinuous arguments, overlapping/reverse-order nuggets, and sub-events — phenomena poorly represented in existing EE datasets.

Extensive and transparent dataset construction and quality-control pipeline is documented (multi-stage annotator training, separated annotation/inspection roles, first-pass acceptance rate, remuneration details), aiding reproducibility.

Thorough statistical comparison against nine other domain-specific EE datasets convincingly demonstrates the higher density and structural complexity of scientific abstracts relative to prior resources.

EXCEEDS offers a clean, unified word-word grid formulation (HTL/THL/EAL relations) that elegantly encodes discontinuous, overlapping, and hierarchical event structures in a single end-to-end model, avoiding pipeline or schema-conditioned generation limitations of baselines.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation against a wide range of global, discriminative, and generative EE baselines, plus ablations, complex-scenario breakdowns, and detailed error analysis (missed vs. boundary errors, confusion patterns), providing good insight into remaining challenges.
Extensive appendices (decoding algorithm, complexity analysis, full P/R/F1 tables, annotation interface screenshots, schema definitions) support reproducibility.
weaknesses: The dataset is built entirely from ACL main-conference abstracts (2019–2022), i.e., a narrow NLP sub-domain; framing this as representative of the general "scientific domain" is an overreach the authors themselves acknowledge only briefly in limitations. The observed density/complexity may partly reflect the specific rhetorical templates of ACL abstracts and the schema designed around them, rather than an intrinsic property of scientific text broadly, weakening the generality of the central claim.

No inter-annotator agreement statistic (e.g., Cohen's/Fleiss' kappa) is reported; only a first-pass inspection acceptance rate (73.05%) is given, which is a weaker and less standard indicator of annotation reliability and dataset quality.

Reported performance gains of EXCEEDS over the strongest baselines are often marginal on the main metrics (e.g., +0.51% AC, +0.53% EC), and absolute AC/AI scores remain modest (~43–45%), raising questions about how much the method itself (versus dataset difficulty) drives the narrative; larger gains appear mainly in complex-structure subsets, which should be more central to the claimed contribution.

The grid-based token-relation approach (HTL/THL/EAL over an l×l grid) is conceptually close to existing word-word relation grid methods used in NER/RE (e.g., W2NER-style formulations); the technical novelty relative to simply adapting such grids to the EE setting is somewhat incremental.

Baseline adaptation choices (e.g., restricting discriminative EAE models to contiguous spans, using different pretrained backbones per model family) could affect fairness of comparison, and it is unclear whether all baselines were adequately hyperparameter-tuned specifically for SciEvents rather than inherited defaults from TextEE.

The evaluation protocol (exact span match, EC metric) is dataset-specific and not benchmarked against established EE evaluation critiques (e.g., Peng et al. 2023, cited but not deeply engaged with), leaving some questions about metric robustness for the newly introduced correlation task.
